question.value: Characterize the early stages of the multi-wavelength afterglow evolution of GRB 190829A and determine its emission mechanism, physics of the ejecta, and properties of the external medium.

evidence.quote: In this work, we present the multi-wavelength Swift observations of GRB 190829A, and complement them with optical data from the MASTER telescopes, and radio data from ATCA and ALMA to fully characterize the early stages of the afterglow evolution.

Results are presented in Section 3 where we discuss the prompt emission properties and the multi-wavelength evolution of the early afterglow, discussing their implications in terms of emission mechanism, physics of the ejecta and properties of the external medium.

findings_qualitative.value: Sensitive upper limits on optical linear polarization disfavor off-axis jet models as the explanation for the delayed X-ray and optical afterglow peak.

evidence.quote: We report sensitive limits on the linear polarization of the optical emission, disfavouring models of off-axis jets to explain the delayed afterglow peak.

findings_qualitative.value: The multi-wavelength afterglow requires at least two emission components: a bright reverse shock dominating early optical/X-ray and high-frequency radio emission, and a forward shock dominating late-time and low-frequency radio emission.

evidence.quote: The study of the multi-wavelength light curves and broadband spectra supports a model with at least two emission components: a bright reverse shock emission, visible at early times in the optical and X-rays and, later, in the radio band; and a forward shock component dominating at later times and lower radio frequencies.

findings_qualitative.value: Standard fireball closure relations for a reverse shock expanding in a constant density medium do not provide an acceptable fit without modifications such as low initial Lorentz factor, high RS-to-FS magnetic field ratio, continued energy injection, or shell interaction.

evidence.quote: By imposing the standard closure relations for a RS expanding in a constant density medium, no acceptable fit could be found.

Although the forward/reverse shock model naturally describes the salient features of the afterglow, its basic version, as described by the standard fireball model and closure relations (cite: vanderHorst2014), does not provide a good fit to the dataset.

findings_qualitative.value: GRB 190829A shares prompt and afterglow energetics with cosmological long GRBs rather than sub-energetic nearby bursts.

evidence.quote: A combined study of the prompt and afterglow properties shows many similarities with cosmological long GRBs, suggesting that GRB 190829A is an example of classical GRBs in the nearby universe.

claims.hypothesis: The delayed X-ray and optical afterglow peak of GRB 190829A is caused by a narrow relativistic jet observed off-axis (theta_v ~ 2 theta_jet).
claims.experiment: Measure optical linear polarization with MASTER between T0+1700 s and T0+6000 s and compare the Stokes Q upper limit with off-axis jet polarization models for homogeneous, power-law, and Gaussian jet profiles.
claims.result: Time-averaged 3-sigma upper limit of Q <= 6%, well below the predictions for off-axis jet emission.
claims.finding: Off-axis jet models with theta_v ~ 2 theta_jet are disfavored with ~90% confidence for a homogeneous jet, ~80% for a power-law jet, and ~70% for a Gaussian jet.

evidence.quote: In this interval, the time-averaged 3 $\sigma$ upper limit is $Q$ $\lesssim$6%, where $Q=\left(F_{0}-F_{90}\right)/\left(F_0 + F_{90}\right)$ is the Stokes parameter

For a randomly oriented polarization vector, the probability of a non detection is however small and we can disfavour the presence of an off-axis jet with $\theta_{v}~\sim~2\theta_{jet}$ with a confidence of $\approx$90% for a homogeneous jet, $\approx$80% for a power-law jet, and $\approx$70% for a Gaussian jet.

claims.hypothesis: The multi-wavelength afterglow of GRB 190829A is produced by a combination of a reverse shock (RS) and a forward shock (FS) expanding in a constant density medium.
claims.experiment: Fit X-ray, UV/optical/nIR, and ALMA/ATCA radio light curves and multi-epoch broadband SEDs with smoothly broken power laws and compare with a single-component standard FS model in afterglowpy.
claims.result: High-frequency ALMA (343 GHz, 100 GHz) and early X-ray/optical light curves show a steep decay (~t^-1.65) underestimated by a single FS model, while low-frequency ATCA (<9 GHz) light curves peak at 4.1 d and decay as t^-1.13.
claims.finding: The broadband evolution is explained by a bright reverse shock dominating early optical/X-ray and high-frequency radio bands and a forward shock dominating low-frequency radio and late emission, though standard RS closure relations require modification.

evidence.loc: A forward shock plus reverse shock scenario
evidence.quote: The steep decay after the break is similar to the post-peak decay observed in the optical and X-rays afterglow (also with index $\sim$1.65). This supports the hypothesis of a common origin for the broadband emission: a bright RS emission initially peaking close to the optical/nIR range, then shifting toward radio wavelengths as it cools off.

evidence.loc: A forward shock plus reverse shock scenario
evidence.quote: As suggested by (cite: Rhodes2020), the low-frequency behavior is consistent with emission from a forward shock expanding into a homogeneous medium.

claims.hypothesis: GRB 190829A is an analogue to cosmological long GRBs rather than a sub-energetic local burst.
claims.experiment: Estimate the blastwave kinetic energy from late-time (14 d) X-ray luminosity and constrain the jet opening angle from the absence of a jet break out to 100 d.
claims.result: E_K,iso ~ 3 x 10^52 erg, theta_j >= 16 deg, and collimation-corrected energy E_K >= 5 x 10^50 erg.
claims.finding: GRB 190829A has a long-lived X-ray afterglow and collimation-corrected energy consistent with the general population of cosmological long GRBs.

evidence.quote: and a collimation-corrected energy release $E_K \gtrsim 5 \times 10^{50} {\rm~erg}$. This value is consistent with the general population of GRBs (cite: Aksulu21) and suggests that, unlike other nearby sub-energetic bursts, GRB 190829A was analogue to the class of cosmological GRBs.

why_this_data.value: Broadband observations from radio (ALMA/ATCA) to optical (MASTER/UVOT) and X-rays (Swift) are needed to characterize the early afterglow evolution and disentangle emission components.

evidence.quote: Broadband observations, from radio to X-rays, of the early afterglow are key to understand the origin of the VHE component.

In this work, we present the multi-wavelength Swift observations of GRB 190829A, and complement them with optical data from the MASTER telescopes, and radio data from ATCA and ALMA to fully characterize the early stages of the afterglow evolution.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Off-axis narrow jet model (Sato et al. 2021) for the delayed afterglow peak, rejected/disfavored due to lack of optical linear polarization

evidence.quote: In all cases with $\theta_{v}~\gtrsim~\theta_{jet}$ our limit is well below the predictions for off-axis jet emission.

The lack of detectable optical polarization allows us to disfavor emission from a misaligned jet with $\theta_{v}\,\gtrsim\,2\theta_{jet}$ (cite: Sato2021), indicating that viewing angle effects can not explain the bright and delayed peak observed at optical and X-ray wavelengths.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: X-ray flare origin for the 1400 s rebrightening, rejected because the rebrightening is achromatic across UV/optical/nIR and X-rays

evidence.loc: A forward shock plus reverse shock scenario
evidence.quote: The sharp temporal rise, $\alpha \sim$-3, and the steep post-peak decay, $\alpha$ $\sim$1.7, are not consistent with the standard evolution of external shock emission, and the achromatic nature of the rebrightening is not typical of X-ray flares either.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Single standard forward shock model for the entire broadband dataset, rejected because it underestimates early X-ray/optical and high-frequency radio emission

evidence.quote: While the late X-rays and low-frequency radio data can be reasonably well described by this FS model, the early time X-rays/optical data and the high-frequency radio emission are significantly underestimated by the model.

limitations_admitted.value: MASTER has only two orthogonal polarizing filters at a single site and measures only Stokes Q, so an unfavorable polarization angle orientation could still hide a polarized afterglow.

evidence.quote: However, each telescope of the MASTER network has two filter with orthogonal polarization angles and can only constrain the component of the polarization vector along the line of sight.
For unfavorable orientations, that is $\Theta$ $\gtrsim$ 1/2 arccos($Q_{UL}$/$P_L$), a highly polarized afterglow could still result in a non-detection (cite: Gorbovskoy2012).

limitations_admitted.value: Standard closure relations for a reverse shock in a constant density medium do not provide an acceptable fit to the SED evolution.

evidence.quote: By imposing the standard closure relations for a RS expanding in a constant density medium, no acceptable fit could be found.

limitations_admitted.value: The estimated isotropic kinetic energy is only a lower limit because the fraction of accelerated electrons xi may be < 1 and Compton losses from the VHE component may suppress X-ray flux.

evidence.quote: Our estimated total energy is an order of magnitude lower than the value derived by (cite: Salafia2021), however we caution that our value can only place a lower limit to the burst energetics.

referee_caveats_inferred: Typo in Equation (1) text where z=0.00785 is printed instead of z=0.0785.
Central frequency of ALMA Band 7 is stated as 335 GHz in text Section 2.5, 343.5 GHz in Table 4, and 343 GHz in Section 3.2.2.

In Table 4, footnote c states that the August 31 at 6:59 UT observation has a central frequency of 97.5 GHz instead of 99.8 GHz, but the 6:59 UT row in Table 4 is the 343.5 GHz observation, while the 97.5/99.8 GHz observation on August 31 is at 9:20 UT.

data_public_as_stated.value: ALMA and ATCA data retrieved from public archives; Swift XRT data retrieved from online repository; article data shared on reasonable request.

evidence.quote: Data were collected from the Atacama Large Millimetre-Submillimetere Array (ALMA) science archive under programs 2018.1.01410.T (PI: Perley) and 2018.1.01454.T (PI: Laskar).
We processed the public dataset through the data reduction package Miriad (cite: Sault1995)
The data underlying this article will be shared on reasonable request to the corresponding author.

products_in_archive.value: Final calibrated ALMA images retrieved from the ALMA science archive.

evidence.quote: For our analysis we used the final calibrated images retrieved from the archive.

Custom scripts or software used to fit the smoothly broken power-law light curves and multi-epoch SEDs

reproducibility.estimated_data_volume_inferred: ~1-5 GB (archival ALMA FITS images for 12 epochs, ATCA continuum visibility datasets, and Swift/UVOT/XRT/BAT files)
reproducibility.score_reason: ALMA analysis uses standard archival calibrated images with straightforward Gaussian fitting in CASA 5.4, and all extracted flux densities are tabulated in Table 4; minor ambiguity in exact fitting regions and custom SED fitting routines.
reproducibility.rediscovery_reason: Public ALMA archival calibrated images exist for both project codes, the measurement recipe (CASA Gaussian fitting + quadrature calibration uncertainty) is simple and well-specified, and all resulting flux densities and light-curve break parameters are explicitly tabulated.
